items.content:
Anthropic Mythos audited Firefox extensively. Their AI agent VEGA still found a JIT bug that pwned both Firefox and Tor Browser.

A single incorrect alias set in SpiderMonkey’s IonMonkey compiler. MObjectToIterator marked as a harmless Load when it actually reallocates property buffers. GVN sees no side effects between two MSlots loads, eliminates the second one. The old pointer is now dangling.

Use-after-free on stale dynamic slots. Spray adjacent objects. Leaked Hidden Class pointer through lazy property resolution landing in the spray. addrof and fakeobj primitives. Fake Uint8Array for arbitrary read/write. Full renderer process compromise.

The first SpiderMonkey JIT CVE after Firefox’s pre-Pwn2Own patch that fixed a large batch of vulnerabilities. Reported May 20. Mozilla fixed it the same day.

https://t.co/LYu1vyPuXP

items.content:
RT @cr3ghost: Every malware analyst and reverse engineer has used x64dbg. Most have no idea what else the creator has been building.

RiscY Business breaks down the practical engineering of building a low-footprint RISC-V virtual machine interpreter for code obfuscation. If you have ever sat in front of a VM-protected sample wondering how the obfuscator was designed, this is the post that answers it. Understanding how these VMs are built is how you learn to tear them apart. Red teamers and implant developers have already been adopting this approach to protect payloads from static analysis, so expect to see more of it in the wild.

Striga lifts x86 to LLVM IR with Python for binary deobfuscation, the same approach used to analyze obfuscation like LummaC2. Bootkitting Windows Sandbox covers UEFI bootkit internals.

TitanHide bypasses anti-debug protections including VMProtect 3.9.4. Dumpulator emulates memory dumps for malware config extraction and unpacking without executing the sample.

He teaches two courses. LLVM IR and Binary Lifting for malware analysts and reverse engineers who need to deobfuscate protected binaries. Payload Obfuscation for Red Teams covering VM-based payload protection, compiling C payloads to RISC-V shellcode, opcode shuffling, instruction encryption, interpreter hardening, and C2 integration.

The attack and the defense. From the same person.

Started reversing in 2009. 100+ open source projects. All free.

items.content:
RT @AretiqAI: CVE-2026-54995: An unauthenticated attacker can send crafted PGM multicast packets to crash Windows at the kernel level — or potentially achieve remote code execution.

The bug: an integer underflow in rmcast.sys's FEC parity counter wraps a byte from 0 to 255, causing out-of-bounds writes into kernel pool memory during FEC decoding.

Affects every supported Windows version (client + server). Microsoft patched it in July 2026 with a validation check before FEC decode — but left the underflow itself intact.

CVSS 8.1 (Microsoft) · Our CVSS 4.0: 7.2 — the attack requires a PGM receiver app to be running (uncommon outside MSMQ/multicast deployments).

Full root cause analysis, annotated disassembly, patch diff, PoC, and detection rules:
https://t.co/jiEtZmEQsZ

Building on ZeroBEC's excellent research into 𝗞𝗮𝗹𝗶𝟯𝟲𝟱 𝗥𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿, and based on intelligence gathered through @anyrun_app , I observed that Kali365 threat actors began leveraging a more sophisticated infrastructure chain as early as 𝗝𝘂𝗻𝗲 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲.

The attack flow abuses trusted cloud services to increase legitimacy and evade detection:
𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗦𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 (𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲) → 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 → 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗚𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝘆 → 𝗖𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗲-𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗞𝗮𝗹𝗶𝟯𝟲𝟱 𝗵𝗼𝘀𝘁

The initial lure is hosted behind a trusted 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗦𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 wrapper before victims are redirected through multiple intermediary services, ultimately landing on the actor-controlled Kali365 infrastructure protected by Cloudflare.

🛡️ 𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Security teams should review 𝗘𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗨𝗿𝗹𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗼 telemetry and look for unusual spikes in:
𝚜𝚒𝚝𝚎𝚜.𝚐𝚘𝚘𝚐𝚕𝚎.𝚌𝚘𝚖/𝚟𝚒𝚎𝚠
with:

items.content:
RT @cr3ghost: Any domain user. Domain Controller certificate. Full domain compromise. One Python script. Default configuration.

Certighost (CVE-2026-54121, CVSS 8.8) abuses the AD CS enrollment chase fallback. The CA reads an attacker-controlled `cdc` attribute and follows it to a rogue host without ever checking if the target is a real Domain Controller.

Create a machine account via the default MachineAccountQuota. Spin up rogue LDAP and SMB listeners. The CA connects back, authenticates through the real DC via Netlogon, but your rogue LDAP returns the target DC's objectSid and dNSHostName instead. The CA issues a valid Domain Controller certificate.

PKINIT with the DC's PFX. DCSync the entire domain. Extract krbtgt. Game over.

Works with the default Machine template and default ACLs. No special configuration required.

Patched July 14, 2026. PoC dropped yesterday. If your AD CS hosts are not patched, this is your priority.

Temporary mitigation: certutil -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC

https://t.co/Cyj7qTXY7V

Authors: @h0j3n @aniqfakhrul

#ActiveDirectory #InfoSec #BlueTeam

items.content:
RT @calif_io: Apple MIE exploitation challenge:
https://t.co/WlnrCkW6Gw

Two months ago, we demonstrated the first public bypass of Apple MIE on macOS 26.4.1. We withheld the technical details until Apple shipped fixes, which are now available in macOS 26.6. We'd like to thank Apple for their collaboration throughout this disclosure process. Since March, we've reported 38 vulnerabilities to Apple and counting.

In this blog, we'll share the details of the two vulnerabilities behind our exploit. We'll present the full exploit at Black Hat USA on August 5 and publish the complete technical report afterward.

Before then, we'd like to turn these bugs into a challenge. Apple MIE combines defenses across hardware, the hypervisor, the kernel, and userspace. Together, they form a mesh of overlapping filters that block many classes of vulnerabilities. Apple also continues to strengthen these mitigations over time. 

Given their complexity, rapid evolution, and the limited public discussion of exploitation techniques, we believe modern XNU kernel exploitation is one of the hardest and most interesting benchmarks for AI-assisted exploit development. We'd love to see how the community solves this challenge before we reveal our own approach at Black Hat. Humans, AI, and human-AI teams are all welcome.

We're looking forward to seeing different solutions and learning new techniques. It took us about five days to go from bug discovery to a polished exploit for this chain.
